paras: The expulsion of Pauline Willis from Yazoo City was the forcing out of a young Black woman from Yazoo City, Mississippi, in early 1919 because she sold Black newspapers there. No violence was reported, but Black weeklies from St. Louis to Milwaukee carried the story as an example of white efforts to keep the race press out of the South.

Willis worked as an agent for the St. Louis Argus, and the Cleveland Advocate described her as "an energetic and bright young Colored woman" of the city. In the same weeks the Baltimore Afro-American reported that a Yazoo minister, Rev. Thomas Collins, had fled the town and said that white people had ordered that no race literature be circulated in the town.

By March 3, 1919, Willis had left Yazoo City, according to a message from the town that the Argus printed that week. The message said she "was compelled to leave on account of selling Colored cameras," an apparent error for papers. A Yazoo City dispatch dated March 25 said she had "persisted in selling race newspapers" and that local "crackers" compelled her to go. Neither account names the people who forced her out or says how they did so.
No report of an arrest or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The Argus ran the message it received without comment under the headline "News Dealer Has to Leave Southern Town." The Cleveland Advocate headed its item "Can You Beat This?" and set the expulsion against white talk of "world democracy," saying the "stiff neck 'crackers'" did not want papers "that protest against injustice" circulated. The Philadelphia Tribune reprinted the Advocate's wording on April 19 under "Driven Away From Home for Selling Race Papers," and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade gave a one-sentence notice on April 26.

The Tribune's text, garbled in places, gives her name as "Miss Jaime Willis, an encyclopedia editor of this city" and redates the story to April 15. The name Pauline appears in the three other reports, including the earliest, sent to her employer, and "encyclopedia editor" stands where the Advocate has "energetic and bright young Colored woman."

reader.title: Expulsion of Pauline Willis from Yazoo City
bases: A young Black woman was 'compelled to leave' (A1, A2) or 'ordered to leave town' (A6) for selling Black newspapers; no violence is reported.
A message from Yazoo City to her employer (A1) and a separately worded Yazoo City dispatch (A2), echoed by a tabloid item (A6), agree that Pauline Willis was forced out for selling race newspapers.

accounts.label: Message to the St. Louis Argus
accounts.gist: An unsigned message from Yazoo City dated March 3 told the Argus that its agent Pauline Willis was no longer in town and had been compelled to leave for selling its papers.

accounts.label: Yazoo City dispatch
accounts.gist: A March 25 dispatch said 'crackers' who talked loudest about world democracy compelled Miss Pauline Willis to leave because she persisted in selling race papers that protest against injustice.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate headed the item 'Can You Beat This?' and mocked the 'stiff neck "crackers"' who talked of world democracy while barring race papers.
The St. Louis Argus printed the message it received under 'News Dealer Has to Leave Southern Town' without comment.
The Philadelphia Tribune reprinted the Advocate's wording under 'Driven Away From Home for Selling Race Papers'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Blade gave a one-sentence tabloid notice.

conflicts.note: The Tribune text is an OCR-garbled reprint of the Advocate wording; 'Pauline' is given by three papers including the earliest, a message to her employer, and is the better reading.

versions.value: Argus agent / seller of race newspapers; 'energetic and bright young Colored woman'

conflicts.note: 'Encyclopedia editor' stands where the Advocate has 'energetic and bright young Colored woman' and appears to be a garble of it.
The later datelines belong to the dispatch and its reprint; the March 3 message shows she had already left by then.

record_check.dossier: One victim, Pauline Willis; 'Jaime' is a garbled reprint variant

record_check.record: Miss Jaime Willis, an encyclopedia editor ...
record_check.dossier: Pauline Willis, a young Black woman and agent for the St. Louis Argus, was forced out of Yazoo City for selling race newspapers

info: On or before March 3, 1919 (date of the message from Yazoo City reporting she had left)
Pauline Willis, described as a young Colored woman of Yazoo City and agent for the St. Louis Argus
No crime alleged; she was forced out for persisting in selling race newspapers
Unnamed local whites, called 'crackers' by the Cleveland Advocate dispatch

sources.note: Earliest report: prints a message dated Yazoo City, March 3, saying the Argus's agent Pauline Willis was compelled to leave town for selling 'Colored cameras' [papers].
quotes: This is to let you know that your agent, Pauline Willis is not in town any more. She was compelled to leave on account of selling Colored cameras.

sources.note: Yazoo City dispatch dated March 25, 'Can You Beat This?': 'crackers' compelled Miss Pauline Willis to leave for persisting in selling race newspapers.
quotes: the "crackers" down here who have been talking loudest about world democracy compelled he rto leave the city
The stiff neck "crackers" in this vicinity do not want race papers that protest against injustice to be circulated here.

sources.note: Rev. Thomas Collins fled Yazoo after the white Commercial Club ordered him whipped; reports whites had ordered no race literature circulated in Yazoo. Does not name Willis.
quotes: White people had ordered that no race literature be circulated in Yazoo

sources.note: Garbled reprint of the Advocate wording under 'Driven Away From Home for Selling Race Papers', redated April 15; names 'Miss Jaime Willis, an encyclopedia editor'.
quotes: Because Miss Jaime Willis, an encyclopedia editor of this city, persisted in selling race newspapers here

sources.note: One-sentence tabloid item: Miss Pauline Willis, a young colored woman, ordered to leave Yazoo for selling colored newspapers.
quotes: Because of her activity in selling colored newspapers here, Miss Pauline Willis, a young colored woman, has been ordered to leave town.

set_aside: Editorial mentions the Yazoo minister who faced a whipping post for reading colored newspapers; no mention of Willis.
